p.s: E.4 Calculating Analysts Beliefs about Fund Returns
p.t: We calculate analysts' expectations of fund returns based on fund holdings and analysts' price targets for individual equities. To begin, we construct expected returns at the individual share level. This is done by dividing the analyst's 12-month price target by the current share price and subtracting one. For each stock, we calculate the mean and standard deviation of all estimates in a given quarter, resulting in a dataset organized by ticker and quarter. To address the presence of outliers in analysts' estimates, we exclude observations where the analyst's implied expected returns exceed 100%. Next, we merge our ticker-by-quarter level analyst expectations data with quarterly data on equity mutual fund holdings, as reported on Form 12S. We calculate fund-level implied expected returns by taking weighted averages of the ticker-level estimates. The weight on share s for fund k in quarter q is determined by the fraction of k's holdings invested in share s for which we have analyst estimates in quarter q. We calculate fund-level implied standard deviations of expected returns, assuming that expected returns are independent across fund holdings. Lastly, we compare our fund-level analyst expectations with our estimates of investor beliefs. Since our investor data is annual and our analyst beliefs data is quarterly, we utilize the analysts' beliefs as of the second quarter, which is roughly halfway through the year. Because many funds in our sample hold bonds and other non-equity securities, and our analyst beliefs data only pertains to equities, we limit our focus to those fund-quarter observations where we have expected returns data for at least 80% of portfolio holdings (weighted by AUM). We remove outliers by excluding observations in both the bottom and top 5% of the distributions of the mean and the standard deviation of fund-level analyst expectations.

We find in Section 5 that, while there is a large dispersion in beliefs across investors, the welfare costs associated with this dispersion are modest. One reason is that we focus on 401(k) holdings, which consist primarily of well-diversified mutual funds. This investment setting reduces the scope for large welfare losses from suboptimal asset allocations. To illustrate this point, we consider a counterfactual exercise where investors allocate across individual stocks. We compare allocations based on heterogeneous beliefs and common beliefs, and find that the welfare cost of belief distortions in this context are an order of magnitude larger than in 401(k) settings. Specifically, instead of funds, we assume investors allocated across individual stocks held by mutual funds on their plan menus. To form stock allocation under heterogeneous belief ω s mt , we use beliefs about stock returns based on the factor structure of stocks and the factor beliefs estimated in Section 4.2.2. We measure beliefs about stock k for investors in plan m at time t as: Next, we consider the counterfactual scenario in which all investors share the same beliefs about stock returns, µ s t , which are again linear combinations of stock factor loadings and estimated common factor beliefs. To estimate common factor beliefs, we regress the common belief µ t in our fund counterfactual in Section 5 on fund factor loadings. Using these common beliefs, we compute the optimal portfolio ω s mt , and evaluate changes in consumer surplus between ω s mt and ω s mt following eq. ( 10). Similar to the counterfactual exercise in Section 5, we use plan specific risk aversion to compute both ω s mt and ω s mt . Due to the large number of individual stocks, this counterfactual is more computationally demanding, so we randomly draw 20% of plans in 2016 and restrict to plans with fewer than 1000 unique stocks.

Figure A5 illustrates much larger costs of belief distortion, when investors allocate across individual stocks instead of diversified mutual funds. In this stock counterfactual, the welfare cost of belief distortion is on average 7.5%, with a median of 4.7%. One reason is that individual stocks are further away from the efficient frontier.
